title: Aidiachtaí agus céimeanna comparáide

rules.point: an aidiacht: na dóigheanna lena húsáid
rules.text: An adjective can be used in three ways: after the verb tá as a predicate (Tá sé tuirseach), in a copula exclamation of the shape Is + adjective + an + noun + é (Is deas an rothar é), or directly after the noun it describes (bean bhocht, asal beag dubh).

rules.point: an aidiacht i ndiaidh ainmfhocail bhaininscnigh: séimhiú
rules.text: When the adjective follows a feminine singular noun it is lenited (bean bhocht, girseach bheag); after a masculine noun it is not (asal beag dubh, gasúr beag). This also holds after a preposition and the article, where Ulster lenites the noun as well: ar an bhean chráifeach (the book's standard form is ar an mbean chráifeach). It matters for the gap exercises (an bhean chráifeach, obair shealadach, ócáid bhliantúil, áit fhothainiúil).

rules.point: céimeanna comparáide: breischéim agus sárchéim
rules.text: The comparative is formed with níos plus the comparative form of the adjective (Tá Séamas níos airde) and the superlative with is plus the same form (Is é Tomás an duine is airde). The comparative form is the same in both degrees.

rules.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí a chríochnaíonn ar chonsan leathan
rules.text: For a plain adjective ending in a broad consonant, slenderise the final consonant and add -e: ard becomes airde. Other examples given: bán, bocht, bog, caol, dearg, fuar, glas (báine, boichte, boige, caoile, deirge, fuaire, glaise).

rules.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí ar -ach agus -each
rules.text: An adjective ending in -ach changes -ach to -aí, and one ending in -each changes -each to -í: feargach becomes feargaí, díreach becomes dírí.

rules.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí ar -úil
rules.text: An adjective ending in -úil adds -a: éirimiúil becomes éirimiúla, cairdiúil becomes cairdiúla.

rules.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí ar -mhar agus -ar
rules.text: An adjective ending in -mhar (or -ar) adds -e with slenderisation: luachmhar becomes luachmhaire, lúfar becomes lúfaire.

rules.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí a gcailltear guta iontu (coimriú)
rules.text: Some two-syllable adjectives drop the vowel of the last syllable and add -e: ramhar becomes raimhre. The same type: folamh, daingean, íseal, uasal, álainn, domhain, saibhir, deacair, aoibhinn (foilmhe, daingne, ísle, uaisle, áille, doimhne, saibhre, deacra, aoibhne). The page image confirms the book prints domhan (the noun for world); the adjective meaning deep is domhain, and the app should use domhain. Ulster usage is the same as the standard here.

rules.point: comparáid chothrom: chomh ... le
rules.text: To say as ... as, use chomh with the basic form of the adjective, not the comparative form, followed by le (Níl Muiris chomh fiosrach le Liam) or by is a (Níl sé chomh ceomhar anocht is a bhí sé aréir). Note that le followed by the article lenites in Ulster: chomh ceanúil leis an mhadadh.

rules.point: breischéim: níos ... ná, i bhfad níos
rules.text: The thing compared is introduced with ná (Tá an áit seo níos contúirtí ná an áit eile), and i bhfad before níos strengthens the comparison (Tá ola i bhfad níos flúirsí anois). In Ulster níos is used in past-tense sentences too (Bhí an leabhar eile níos greannmhaire), so the book's practice suits the school and ní ba need not be taught.

rules.point: aidiachtaí a bhfuil breischéim ar leith acu
rules.text: A small group of common adjectives has an irregular comparative form that must be learnt: maith, níos fearr; olc, níos measa; mór, níos mó; beag, níos lú; fada, níos faide; furast, níos fusa; te, níos teo; tréan, níos treise or níos tréine; breá, níos breátha. The same form follows is in the superlative. Furast is the Ulster spelling the book already uses (standard furasta).

title: An chéad díochlaonadh: iolraí agus tuiseal ginideach

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, iolraí laga: caolú
rules.text: Most weak plurals in the first declension are formed simply by making the final consonant of the word slender, for example bád becomes báid.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, iolraí laga: -a a chur leis
rules.text: Some first-declension plurals are formed by adding -a to the word, for example ceart becomes cearta.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, tréaniolraí
rules.text: Some words in this group have strong plurals, for example dán becomes dánta and cogadh becomes cogaí.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, inscne
rules.text: All first-declension nouns are masculine.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, deireadh an fhocail
rules.text: First-declension nouns end in a broad consonant.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha
rules.text: The nominative singular is made slender to form the genitive singular, and the noun is lenited after the article where possible, for example an capall gives cosa an chapaill. This is the same in Ulster: the genitive singular after an lenites b, c, f, g, m and p, and leaves d and t alone (fear an tí, doras an dorais).

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach iolra
rules.text: The genitive plural has the same form as the nominative singular, and after na it is eclipsed where possible, for example seolta na mbád, cosa na gcapall (the book shows this in its examples rather than stating it). Ulster does not differ here: eclipsis after na in the genitive plural is standard everywhere.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, focail a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rules.text: Nouns beginning with a vowel take t- in the nominative singular (an t-úll), nothing in the genitive singular (dath an úill), h in the nominative plural (na húlla, na hoileáin) and n- in the genitive plural (dath na n-úll, muintir na n-oileán).

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, focail a thosaíonn ar s + guta
rules.text: Nouns beginning with s followed by a vowel take t before the s in the genitive singular after the article (cóta an tsagairt, doras an tséipéil) but are unchanged in the genitive plural (cótaí na sagart, doirse na séipéal).

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, focail a chríochnaíonn ar -ach, -each
rules.text: Nouns ending in -ach or -each change that ending to -aigh or -igh in the genitive singular and the nominative plural (an marcach, cáipín an mharcaigh, na marcaigh), while the genitive plural keeps the -ach form with eclipsis (cáipíní na marcach, oifigí na gcléireach).

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn ea go i
rules.text: When the noun has ea before the final consonant, ea changes to i in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an fear, teach an fhir, na fir, tithe na bhfear.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn éa go éi
rules.text: When the noun has éa before the final consonant, éa changes to éi in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an páipéar, dath an pháipéir, na páipéir, dath na bpáipéar. The book's box heading reads ÉA to Í, but every example shows éa becoming éi.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn íoch go igh
rules.text: Nouns ending in -íoch change that ending to -igh in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an beithíoch, luach an bheithígh, na beithígh, luach na mbeithíoch. Beithíoch is a very common Ulster word for a cow or a beast, so pupils will meet it often.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn ia go éi
rules.text: When the noun has ia before the final consonant, ia changes to éi in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an t-iasc, praghas an éisc, na héisc, praghas na n-iasc.

title: An tríú díochlaonadh: iolraí agus tuiseal ginideach

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -anna
rules.text: Some third-declension nouns form their plural by adding -anna to the word: rang becomes ranganna.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -í
rules.text: Most third-declension nouns, including the agent nouns in -éir, -eoir, -óir, -úir and abstract nouns in -acht and -int, form their plural by adding -í: cainteoir becomes cainteoirí, beannacht becomes beannachtaí, canúint becomes canúintí.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -acha
rules.text: Some third-declension nouns form their plural by adding -acha to the word: barúil becomes barúlacha.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -ta, -te
rules.text: Some third-declension nouns form their plural by adding -ta or -te to the word: gleann becomes gleannta.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, inscne
rules.text: The third declension contains both masculine and feminine nouns.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, deireadh an fhocail
rules.text: Every noun in the third declension ends in a consonant.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: -a
rules.text: The genitive singular is formed by adding -a to the word. If the final consonant is slender it is made broad first: éir becomes éara, eoir becomes eora, óir becomes óra, úir becomes úra.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: io go ea
rules.text: In one-syllable words the vowel group io changes to ea in the genitive: sioc gives seaca (ag cur seaca), fios gives feasa (ag lorg feasa).

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: focail ar -int
rules.text: In words ending in -int the t is dropped after broadening in the genitive: tuiscint becomes tuisceana.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: focail ar -irt
rules.text: In words ending in -irt the t becomes tha after broadening in the genitive: buairt becomes buartha.

rules.point: an tuiseal ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha
rules.text: The genitive case follows a verbal noun: ag ól fíona, ag foghlaim an cheachta.
